rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midpoint temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Test whether higher temperature improves selectivity for the early critical pair while retaining the same gradient for comparison. The other pairs have substantial resolution margins, and higher temperature should shorten retention.
The maximum CRF has been reached; shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. The early pair at R = 1.67 is the main constraint to monitor.

Narrow the gradient window to recover early-pair resolution at the shorter gradient duration. The resulting slope lies between the two tested slopes, targeting R ≥ 1.5 while keeping the last peak earlier than in injection 2.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 4’s slope to shorten retention and test the early pair’s sensitivity to starting composition. Injection 4 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method if this shift sacrifices resolution.

Test the unexplored low-temperature selectivity regime, where a reversal of the early pair could offer another route to full resolution. Keeping injection 4’s gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect; its CRF 1.000 method remains the fallback.

Explore a faster low-temperature gradient: the early pair’s strong resolution at 25 °C provides room for compression, while a modest temperature increase and steeper slope may separate the late cluster. The higher endpoint also ensures a strong final elution condition.

Use a slope just steeper than injection 4 to seek a slightly faster method while preserving full resolution of the early pair. The last peak previously exited near 0.57 organic, so a 0.70 endpoint should still keep every peak inside the gradient.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 8, targeting early-pair resolution just above 1.5. The last compound may elute during the final hold, but its large separation margin makes this a reasonable test of a shorter gradient.

Test whether a steeper gradient separates the low-temperature late cluster while retaining enough early-pair resolution. This explores a potentially faster alternative; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed method with CRF 1.000.

Explore an intermediate-temperature window to separate the late cluster seen at 25–30 °C. Raising the starting organic fraction also tests whether early-pair selectivity can improve in this regime while shortening overall retention.

Use a shallower gradient and lower starting organic fraction to recover resolution of the early pair at 35 °C. The late pairs were already resolved in injection 11, so this tests a second temperature regime for complete separation.

Return to the successful high-temperature regime and reduce the slope relative to injection 5 to recover early-pair resolution. This tests whether a higher starting composition can provide another CRF 1.000 method with a shorter retention window.

Test a slope just above injection 9’s to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary at 60 °C. The stronger endpoint keeps the last peak inside the gradient, but the early pair’s R = 1.51 leaves little margin.

Test whether a higher starting composition improves early-pair selectivity at 35 °C while preserving the late-pair separation. The slope matches injection 12, isolating the starting-composition effect for peaks eluting within the gradient.

Refine the successful higher-starting-composition method with a slope slightly steeper than injection 13, targeting early-pair resolution near 1.5. This should retain maximum CRF while modestly shortening retention relative to injection 13.

Test a shallower gradient at 30 °C to spread the late critical pairs, with a higher starting composition to offset the added retention. The early pair may benefit from the lower temperature relative to injection 15; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a higher starting composition with a compensating shallower slope to preserve early-pair resolution at 60 °C. This probes whether shifting the elution window can shorten the fully resolved separation beyond injection 9.

Refine the 35 °C alternative with a shallower slope than injection 11 to bring the early pair above R = 1.5 while preserving late-pair resolution. The endpoint should keep the last peak near the end of the gradient and below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 19 to lift its early pair above R = 1.5, while raising the endpoint to avoid hold-related delay of the last peak. This targets a fully resolved lower-temperature alternative with the last peak still within 10 minutes.

Trim the high-temperature gradient endpoint while making the slope slightly shallower than injection 16 to add resolution margin to its borderline early pair. The last peak should remain inside the gradient, targeting CRF 1.000 with an eight-minute program.

Preserve injection 2’s successful gradient slope while trimming the endpoint and programmed duration to the observed elution window. This targets CRF 1.000 with more early-pair resolution margin than the fastest method, injection 9.

Narrow injection 22’s window one step to increase the early pair’s resolution margin while keeping the last peak near eight minutes. Maximum CRF is already established; this tests a more robust fully resolved alternative to the faster but borderline injection 9.

Test a slightly shallower slope to balance the early pair’s improving resolution against the narrowing third–fourth pair, targeting a larger minimum-resolution margin. The last peak is expected before 10 minutes, preserving maximum CRF; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Slightly steepen injection 24’s slope to shorten retention and balance its two limiting pairs near R = 2, while trimming the endpoint to the elution window. This targets maximum CRF with a larger resolution margin than injection 9, which remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
